      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Sleep</span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt2">Narcolepsy</span></content>
      <content name="altTitle">Night Terrors</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sleeping Pills</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">sleep</span>?<p>While you are sleeping  your brain and body functions are still active. <span class="qt1">Sleep</span> is a natural process that helps your body restore energy, supports learning and memory, and keeps you healthy.</p><p>It's not just the number of hours of <span class="qt1">sleep</span> you get that matters. The quality of your <span class="qt1">sleep</span> is also important. During the night, your brain cycles through different stages of non-rapid eye movement (non-REM) <span class="qt1">sleep</span> and rapid eye movement (REM) <span class="qt1">sleep</span>. If your <span class="qt1">sleep</span> is often interrupted, you may not get enough time in certain stages of <span class="qt1">sleep</span>. Poor-quality <span class="qt1">sleep</span> does more than make you feel tired. It can affect your physical and mental health, thinking, and daily functioning.</p>What are <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders?<p><span class="qt1">Sleep</span> disorders are conditions that disturb your normal <span class="qt1">sleep</span> patterns. There are many types of <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders. Some general types include:</p><ul><li>Insomnia, which is trouble falling <span class="qt1">asleep</span> or staying <span class="qt1">asleep</span>.</li><li><span class="qt1">Sleep</span>-related breathing disorders such as <span class="qt1">sleep</span> apnea, a condition in which you stop breathing for 10 seconds or more during <span class="qt1">sleep</span>.</li><li><span class="qt1">Sleep</span>-related movement disorders such as restless leg syndrome (RLS), which involves tingling or prickling sensations in your legs, and a strong urge to move them.</li><li>Hypersomnia, which is extreme daytime sleepiness. This includes <span class="qt2">narcolepsy</span>.</li><li>Circadian rhythm <span class="qt1">sleep</span>-wake disorders, which are problems falling <span class="qt1">asleep</span> or waking up at the right times. This may be due to shift work or jet lag.</li><li>Parasomnia, which is unusual behaviors during <span class="qt1">sleep</span> or while falling <span class="qt1">asleep</span> or waking up. This may include sleepwalking, talking, or eating during <span class="qt1">sleep</span>.</li></ul><p>Some people who feel tired during the day have a true <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorder, while others simply don't get enough <span class="qt1">sleep</span>. The amount of <span class="qt1">sleep</span> you need depends on your age, lifestyle, health, and <span class="qt1">sleep</span> patterns. Most adults need about 7-9 hours each night.</p>What causes <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders?<p>There are different causes for different <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders. They may include:</p><ul><li>Other health conditions, such as heart disease, lung disease, nerve disorders, or pain</li><li>Mental illnesses, including depression and anxiety</li><li>Medicines</li><li>Genetics</li></ul><p>Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p><p>Other factors that may contribute to <span class="qt1">sleep</span> problems include:</p><ul><li>Using caffeine or alcohol</li><li>Having an irregular schedule, such as working the night shift</li><li>Aging, since older adults may <span class="qt1">sleep</span> less, spend less time in deep <span class="qt1">sleep</span>, and wake easily</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders?<p>The symptoms of <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders depend on the specific disorder. Some signs that you may have a <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorder include that:</p><ul><li>You regularly take more than 30 minutes to fall <span class="qt1">asleep</span>.</li><li>You regularly wake up several times and then have trouble falling back to <span class="qt1">sleep</span>, or you wake up too early in the morning.</li><li>You often feel sleepy during the day, take frequent naps, or fall <span class="qt1">asleep</span> at the wrong times during the day.</li><li>Your bed partner says that when you <span class="qt1">sleep</span>, you snore loudly, snort, gasp, make choking sounds, or stop breathing for short periods.</li><li>You have creeping or tingling sensations in your legs or arms that are relieved by moving or massaging them, especially in the evening and when trying to fall <span class="qt1">asleep</span>.</li><li>Your bed partner notices that your legs or arms jerk often during <span class="qt1">sleep</span>.</li><li>You have vivid, dreamlike experiences while falling <span class="qt1">asleep</span> or dozing.</li><li>You have episodes of sudden muscle weakness triggered by strong emotions.</li><li>You feel as though you cannot move or speak for a brief time when you first wake up.</li></ul>How are <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders diagnosed?<p>To diagnose a <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorder, your health care provider will review your medical and <span class="qt1">sleep</span> history and do a physical exam. You may also have a <span class="qt1">sleep</span> study (polysomnogram). Most <span class="qt1">sleep</span> studies  monitor and record data about your body during a full night of <span class="qt1">sleep</span>. The data includes:</p><ul><li>Brain wave activity</li><li>Eye movements</li><li>Breathing rate</li><li>Blood pressure</li><li>Heart rate and electrical activity in the heart and other muscles</li></ul><p>Other types of <span class="qt1">sleep</span> studies may check how quickly you fall <span class="qt1">asleep</span> during daytime naps or how well you can stay awake during the day.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders?<p>Treatments for <span class="qt1">sleep</span> disorders depend on which disorder you have. They may include:</p><ul><li>Practicing good <span class="qt1">sleep</span> habits and other lifestyle changes, such as eating a healthy diet and getting regular exercise</li><li>Reducing anxiety about <span class="qt1">sleep</span> with cognitive behavioral therapy or relaxation techniques</li><li>Using a CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) machine for <span class="qt1">sleep</span> apnea</li><li>Using bright light therapy (in the morning)</li><li>Taking <span class="qt1">sleep</span> aid medicines, or natural products such as melatonin</li></ul><p>Always check with your provider before taking any medicine or supplement. Most <span class="qt1">sleep</span> aid medicines are generally for short-term use.</p></content>

      <content name="title">Degenerative Nerve Diseases</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Ataxia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Neurodegenerative Diseases</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Prion Diseases</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Degenerative nerve diseases affect many of your body's activities, such as balance, movement, talking, breathing, and heart function.   Many of these diseases are genetic. Sometimes the cause is a medical condition such as alcoholism, a tumor, or a stroke. Other causes may include toxins, chemicals, and viruses.  Sometimes the cause is unknown.</p><p>Degenerative nerve diseases include:</p><ul><li>Alzheimer's disease</li><li>Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis</li><li>Friedreich ataxia</li><li>Huntington's disease</li><li>Lewy body disease</li><li>Parkinson's disease</li><li>Spinal muscular atrophy</li></ul><p>Degenerative nerve diseases can be serious or life-threatening. It depends on the type. Most of them have no cure. Treatments may help improve symptoms, relieve pain, and increase mobility.</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/arrhythmia.html">
      <content name="title">Arrhythmia</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Bradycardia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Irregular Heartbeat</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Sick Sinus Syndrome</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Tachycardia</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is an arrhythmia?<p>An arrhythmia is a problem with the rate or rhythm of your heartbeat. Your heart beats too quickly, too slowly, or with an irregular pattern. Changes in the electrical signals that control your heartbeat cause arrhythmias.</p><ul><li>When your heart beats faster than normal, it's called tachycardia.</li><li>When your heart beats too slowly, it's called bradycardia.</li><li>When the signal to beat comes too early, it's called a premature or extra heartbeat. It may feel like your heart skipped a beat.</li></ul><p>There are many types of arrhythmias. Arrhythmias may affect the upper or lower chamber of your heart. The most common type of arrhythmia is atrial fibrillation, which causes an irregular and fast heartbeat.</p><p>Some arrhythmias are harmless, such as when your heart rate speeds up during exercise and slows down when you <span class="qt1">sleep</span>. But if you have a frequent irregular rhythm, it may mean your heart isn't pumping enough blood into your body. Getting treatment and following a heart-healthy lifestyle can help control arrhythmias. It may also help prevent heart damage that can trigger some heart arrhythmias.</p>What causes an arrhythmia?<p>Many factors can affect your heart's rhythm, such as having had a heart attack, smoking, congenital heart defects, and stress. Other factors that could increase your risk for some types of arrhythmias could include if you:</p><ul><li>Have a family history of arrhythmias</li><li>Have certain health conditions, which can include heart and blood vessel diseases, lung diseases, kidney diseases, obesity, and <span class="qt1">sleep</span> apnea</li><li>Are an older adult</li><li>Have had recent surgery for your heart, lungs, or throat</li><li>Take certain medicines for other health conditions</li><li>Use illegal drugs</li></ul><p>If you have risk factors, some situations that make your heart work harder, raise your blood pressure, or cause strong emotional stress may trigger an arrhythmia.</p>What are the symptoms of an arrhythmia?<p>You may not have any noticeable symptoms of an arrhythmia. Your provider may find an arrhythmia during your routine checkup. Symptoms of an arrhythmia can include:</p><ul><li>Fast or slow heartbeat</li><li>Skipping, fluttering, or pounding heartbeats</li><li>Chest pain or discomfort</li><li>Dizziness or fainting</li><li>Shortness of breath</li><li>Sweating</li><li>Tiredness or weakness</li></ul><p>Seek emergency medical care if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or think you are having a heart attack.</p>How is an arrhythmia diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have an arrhythmia, your health care provider may order an electrocardiogram (EKG).  This test records your heart's electrical activity and is the most common for finding an arrhythmia. Your provider may also:</p><ul><li>Ask about your medical history, including your symptoms and lifestyle habits</li><li>Do a physical exam, which includes checking your heartbeat and pulse</li><li>Order blood tests and other heart tests</li><li>Check your legs or feet for swelling</li><li>Look for signs of other health conditions that could cause an arrhythmia, such as thyroid disease</li></ul>What are the treatments for an arrhythmia?<p>Treatment may include medicines, an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) or pacemaker, or sometimes surgery. Your provider may also recommend avoiding activities that may trigger your arrhythmia.</p><p>The goal of treatment is to restore a normal heart rhythm. If not treated, arrhythmias can damage your heart, brain, and other organs and could be life-threatening.</p>Can arrhythmias be prevented?<p>To help prevent an arrhythmia, your provider may suggest that you make heart-healthy lifestyle changes and treat health conditions that may cause arrhythmias.</p><p>NIH: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute</p></content>
